nameStory: The two-striped grasshopper gets its name from the pair of pale yellowish stripes that run down its back like racing stripes on a car. These distinctive stripes make it easy to pick out from the crowd of grasshoppers bouncing around summer meadows.
description: The two-striped grasshopper is a medium-sized hopping insect that's one of New England's most common grasshoppers. Adults typically measure about an inch to inch-and-a-half long, with powerful hind legs built for jumping and relatively short antennae compared to crickets. Their bodies range from brown to green, but those telltale twin stripes down the back are their signature feature. Like all grasshoppers, they're herbivores that munch on grasses and other plants.

idTips.label: Twin back stripes
idTips.description: Two pale yellowish or cream-colored stripes run parallel down the back from head to wing tips - they feel slightly raised if you gently touch them

idTips.label: Body coloration
idTips.description: Overall brown, tan, or greenish body that feels smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, often matching the dried grasses where they live

idTips.label: Short antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are noticeably shorter than the body length and feel thread-like rather than the thick, club-like antennae of some other insects

idTips.label: Powerful hind legs
idTips.description: Large, muscular back legs with spiny edges that feel rough when handled - these legs are disproportionately large compared to the front legs

idTips.label: Wing length
idTips.description: Wings typically extend to or slightly beyond the tip of the abdomen and make a papery rustling sound when they jump

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized grasshopper about the length of your thumb, feeling substantial but not heavy when cupped in your hands

habitat: Two-striped grasshoppers thrive in open, sunny areas throughout New England including meadows, prairies, roadsides, and agricultural fields. They particularly favor areas with mixed grasses and weedy plants, from sea level up to moderate elevations in the mountains. You'll often find them in disturbed areas like old fields, pastures, and the grassy edges of hiking trails.

seasonality.spring: Young nymphs begin emerging from overwintered eggs in late spring, looking like tiny versions of adults but without fully developed wings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are most visible and vocal, with males producing their characteristic buzzing calls and both sexes actively feeding and mating.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, with females laying eggs in soil before the first hard frosts kill the adult population.
seasonality.winter: Only eggs survive the winter, buried in soil and waiting for spring warmth to hatch into the next generation.

funFact: Two-striped grasshoppers can leap up to 20 times their own body length in a single bound - that's like a human jumping the length of a basketball court in one hop!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other spur-throat grasshoppers, but remember 'two stripes, two species' - if you see those twin pale stripes down the back, you've found your two-striped grasshopper. Red-legged grasshoppers have reddish hind legs instead of the prominent back stripes.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'short-horned' grasshoppers (referring to their antennae), these insects are actually more closely related to locusts than to long-horned grasshoppers like katydids. The 'spur-throat' part of their group name refers to a small pointed projection on their throat that you'd need a magnifying glass to see clearly.
compareHints: Among its Melanoplus relatives in New England, the two-striped grasshopper is the only one with those distinctive twin pale stripes running down its back. Red-legged grasshoppers have bright reddish hind legs but lack the back stripes, while most other spur-throat grasshoppers have more mottled or uniform coloring without clear striping patterns. The northern spur-throat grasshopper is similar in size but typically has a more uniform brown coloration.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Melanoplus relatives, the Pine Tree Spur-throat stands out for its strong association with coniferous trees, while most others prefer grasses and herbs in open meadows.

Among its Melanoplus relatives, the red-legged grasshopper is distinguished primarily by those characteristic red-orange hind legs, while the two-striped grasshopper has prominent light stripes down its back, and the differential grasshopper is noticeably larger with chevron markings on its hind legs.
Among its Melanoplus relatives, the differential grasshopper is distinguished by its larger, more robust build and those characteristic dark leg markings.

Among its Melanoplus relatives, the Huckleberry Spur-throat is most reliably separated by habitat - Red-legged Grasshoppers prefer more open grassy areas, Two-striped Grasshoppers like agricultural fields, and Pine tree Spur-throats stick to coniferous areas.
